event: MARSOC VXE470 lost lift during the VTOL descent to the PLZ after a low-battery return, did not follow a right correction, hit the deck and an object, and damaged both lift booms.
failure_mode: insufficient lift on the right side during descent (right throttles railed, roll command not followed); suspected ESC damage from overweight operation, not confirmed by teardown
contributing: aircraft flown about 3.9 lb over the 49 lb MGTOW with HD55, Snake Eagle and Mod A kit
possible bad power connection on the right side (not inspected in person)
HD55 and Snake Eagle had no power after the crash (likely crash damage or downstream effect)

evidence.quote: right side throttles were pegged so I suspect that’s the side that wasn’t able to draw full power
It seems more likely an ESC or prop failure (probably ESC) on the right side.
there is a short time where there is a roll transient consistent with not enough lift from the right side
current draw does not look out of the ordinary when compared with other flights.
the customer stated that the weight of the Snake Eagle and the HD55 came out to 9.4 lbs.

team_root_cause:
Aircraft appears to have been flying over MGTOW by ~3.9 lbs. This likely exceeded the capacity of the lift ESC and damaged it. 
Lift system did not have sufficient power to keep the vehicle airborne during the descent.  Likely ESC failure or bad connector.
Based on the throttle (railed for RF) and the current readings (higher for right), it seems the issue is likely due to RF ESC.

would_settle_it.what: Open and inspect the front right ESC (and right boom power connectors) for burned FETs or connector damage; no teardown was done.
Per-motor ESC current, RPM and throttle on the right side through the descent to tell an ESC fault from a prop or CG problem.
Whether this ESC fits the systemic VXE30 VTOL ESC failure pattern.

reasoning: The log review shows the right side throttles railed while a commanded left roll was not followed, which points to too little lift from the right side, and the team named the RF ESC. The customer confirmed about 9.4 lb of payload plus the Mod A kit, so the aircraft was over MGTOW. No ESC or connector was inspected and one engineer noted current draw looked normal, so the evidence narrows the fault to the right side lift system (most likely the RF ESC) but does not confirm the part.
notes: RF mapped to motor 2 (front right) per the convention. The witness says the left boom rear prop area was severely damaged, which is likely impact damage. Only photos of connectors were attached, with no comment on their condition. VA-93 and VA-221 are corrective-action links (lift current limits, alternative ESCs), not cause evidence.

event: E140Z G2 gimbals on several VXE30s (499 in the Alaska demo, 734 in Huntsville testing) caused fixed wing magnetometer interference, gimbal encoder faults and, on 734, arcing between the gimbal mounting plate and the fuselage.
component: E140Z G2 gimbal housing ground and conductive aluminum gimbal mount (P/N 017.43_C3) on carbon plate
failure_mode: ground loop: gimbal power return is tied to its housing and the conductive mount gives a second return path to the airframe, carrying stray current (about 32 mA) that disturbs the magnetometer and gimbal and caused arcing at the mount plate
contributing: paint wearing off the metal mount plate (Global Support view)
second return path through the Silvus radio assembly
magnetic field of the gimbal motors and lens cap magnet also disturbs the mag even with the cable unplugged (VXEP-500)

evidence.quote: Power on after BIT: (meter and probes configured for DC current): Reading ~32 mA flowing from Gimbal to plane
Confirmed gimbal GND is tied to housing
Resistance from ground pin to gimbal base is 3.5 to 4 Ohms
I’ve added two AAR’s from flights on 18January25 that utilized non-conductive mounts on they payload.

The root cause appears to be a ground loop facilitated by the gimbal having internal power and signal grounds tied to the chassis COMBINED with a path to ground on VXE30 through the fuselage and the Silvus.
The interference exists with the cable unplugged, so it is the magnetic fields of the motor interfering with the mag.

team_root_cause: Power return pins seem common with gimbal housing (not ideal, common cause of ground loops)

would_settle_it.file: VXEP-813 + 1034 E140 Octopus VXE30 mag interference suspected Mount Ground Loop.xlsx
would_settle_it.what: Full test matrix quantifying mag interference with conductive vs non-conductive mounts, powered vs unpowered, to separate ground loop current from the gimbal's own magnetic field.

reasoning: Bench tests found the gimbal ground tied to its housing (3.5 to 4 ohms from ground pin to base) and about 32 mA flowing from gimbal to aircraft through the aluminum mount, with tilt encoder faults when mounted and normal behavior when the gimbal sat beside the aircraft. Non-conductive mounts gave good mag checks and two flights with no mag issues. That pins the stray current path to the gimbal housing ground plus the conductive mount. VXEP-500 shows the gimbal motors' magnetic field also disturbs the mag with the cable unplugged, so the ground loop is likely not the only source of mag interference.
notes: Several aircraft and events: 499 (Alaska demo, gimbals SN6219 and SN6086, INS confusion and high bank angles), 734 (Dec 2024 bench tests, Feb 2025 arcing tracked in VXEP-1034), 674 (tests and VXEP-897 launch abort). The Riga EMI email thread in the comments concerns a different gimbal PCB (E140G3) noise problem. Linked FS2-2604/2605/2606 (symptom tickets) were not read; they bear on symptoms, not the cause.

event: MOLSON VXE591 in fuel cell configuration could not climb and steadily lost HLB charge and altitude in cruise, and the operator made a glide emergency landing at an ELZ; the aircraft was recovered.
component: airframe and prop icing (horizontal stab, wing leading edge, lift props)
failure_mode: cruise power (~700 W) above fuel cell output (~450 to 500 W) for about 30 minutes drained the HLB; AP power limit at low SoC prevented the commanded climb
contributing: flight in freezing fog, which the Operations Manual prohibits
AP throttle power limit based on HLB SoC (worked as designed)
fuel cell supplement guidance limited to cruise recommendations
multiple fuel cell start commands sent in preflight

evidence.quote: Aircraft was operated in icing conditions (weather forecast/report provided by
averaging ~700W of power consumption resulting in a decrease of HLB SoC from 70%
likely due to AP power limiting based on HLB
Yesterday, I was reviewing a university publication that estimated a nearly 80% increase in power consumption due to icing of forward propellers
Flight in cold weather with icing conditions

team_root_cause: Required power to maintain forward flight exceeded nominal fuel cell output for ~30mins resulting in depleted hybrid lift battery and subsequent operator initiated glide landing. Flight into known icing conditions likely contributed to higher than normal cruise power (~700W).

would_settle_it.what: Extent of leading edge and prop icing to support icing as the cause of the ~700 W cruise power.

reasoning: The data review shows the fuel cell delivered its rated 450 to 500 W while the aircraft drew about 700 W in orbit, so the HLB drained and the AP power limit stopped the climb. Photos showed ice on the horizontal stab, wing and lift props, the forecast was freezing fog, and pitot and static data looked unobstructed. Icing is the degraded input that best explains the high power, but the power penalty was not quantified, so this is scored as narrowed to the environment.
notes: The aircraft systems (fuel cell, AP power limit) behaved as designed; scored on the degraded input (icing) per the designed-abort rule. RMA-451 was opened in error and holds no findings. Pat Wells closed it as operator error.

event: PMA263 VXE568 turned 180 degrees as the lift booms came on for the RTB landing, flew forward about 50 ft, made a strained noise and nose dived into a field from about 200 ft.
failure_mode: VTOL AP priority inheritance task lockup of flight critical (priority 1) tasks during fixed wing flight, likely triggered by the RTC hanging the I2C bus, so the VTOL landing could not be controlled
contributing: multiple software airworthiness directives (6.2.9, 6.3.4) not applied
RTC updated from GPS time the prior flight and wrong on next startup

evidence.quote: Corresponding VTOL log (VTOL00078) seems to be missing the landing.
The RTC was updated in FW flight prior to the incident and the RTC was incorrect on startup the next time.
Root cause is a known old VTOL processor bug that causes task lockup in flight critical tasks.
This was old software that missed multiple ADs, it was not flight worthy.
Data indicates the VTOL experienced priority inheritance (a known bug fixed in VTOL 1.54) mid fixed wing flight which prevents the priority 1 tasks from running.

team_root_cause: VTOL AP task lockup occurred during fixed wing flight leading to impact with terrain during subsequent VTOL landing attempt. VTOL was using AP 1.53 FW with known Priority Inheritance bug. Most likely an issue with the RTC on the I2C bus given the date was wrong in some logs and there were many instances of the RTC being updated in previous flights. Also this vehicle was using very old SW, multiple ADs were not implemented.

would_settle_it.what: Readable copy of the investigation report; the attached PDF version did not convert (garbled font codes).

attachments_read: 27687_001058 ADS - PMA263 - RMA VXE-568 Misc. Parts.pdf.md
28475_001058 ADS, Inc. - PMA263 - RMA VXE-568 Misc. Parts.pdf.md
reasoning: The XCOMM log shows the VTOL priority 1 data freezing and the VTOL log stopping before the landing, the signature of the priority inheritance lockup known in VTOL AP 1.53 and seen on XKIT-1958. The RTC was updated in the previous flight and read 1900/01/01 on the next startup, which the team ties to an I2C bus hang as the trigger. The software engineers agree, and the aircraft was missing the ADs that fix the bug, so the mechanism is supported by log evidence; the exact trigger (RTC/I2C) remains a most-likely call.
notes: The VXE-568 Incident Investigation.pdf on RMA-435 converted only as glyph codes and could not be read. The customer mishap report is handwritten and mostly illegible. Read RMA form 25214 and treated 25215 as a duplicate of it (same name and size). RMA-435 says the crash was when switching from VTOL to fixed wing, which conflicts with the operator statement (entering VTOL on landing).

event: TIQUILA VXE601 (fuel cell configuration with HD55) came down fast in the final phase of an automatic VTOL landing in 12 to 16 kt surface wind and landed heavily, left wing low, creasing the aft landing pad.
component: wind at or above published limits with wind shear near touchdown
failure_mode: wind lift on the wing drove lift rotor commands to saturate low, degrading attitude and vertical speed control, and about 15 fps of wind shear just before touchdown gave a hard landing
contributing: winds aloft about 30.5 mph against a 30 mph limit, shown on GCS
pause commanded only after touchdown
heavy TOW (about 44 to 45 lb) with HD55

evidence.quote: AP reported Winds aloft ~45fps (~30.5mph). This would be available on GCS to operator. Ops manual limitations are < 30mph.
~15fps wind shear (loss of wind) occurred just prior to landing.
No obvious lift system issues with regard to power.
Landing pause was commanded after vehicle touched down. Both GCS and VTOL captured the command (ruling out a command not being sent/received).
The result as the wind thresholds are met and/or exceeded will be that the lift system motors will saturate low resulting in degraded attitude control.

team_root_cause: Operator commanded pause after vehicle already touched down. Hard landing due to aircraft being operated at / exceeding published environmental (wind) limitations.
reasoning: Logs show winds aloft above the 30 mph limit, about 15 fps of wind shear just before touchdown, and no lift power problem. Both GCS and VTOL logged the pause command, after touchdown, so the command path worked. The engineers explain the saturated-low rotor commands as an effect of wind lift on the wing, so the hard landing comes from flying at or past the wind limit.
notes: The pink payload video after landing was not investigated. Configuration corrected from standard battery to fuel cell in the comments.

event: Pre-MAGNSS VXE724 on a flight test reported a VTOL climb abort / lift system fault during fixed wing flight, froze the SA camera on transition, and on the VTOL landing slowed its descent early at about 100 ft AGL before landing normally.
failure_mode: VTOL AP watchdog resets after simple_tlb_refill_exception, twice, once at transition to fixed wing; separately lrfFusion offset during descent
contributing: center wing with many NCRs including network intermittency between XCOMM and SLA
MCM power cycling from SLA breakout E-fuse trips on the same aircraft (VXEP-723)
LRF fusion offset likely caused the early slow descent

evidence.quote: trace: func(0) system 6 indicates that simple_tlb_refill_exception happened twice, once during flight as it transitioned to FW flight.
This is the only known WDT to have occurred on this version of software.
At 100ft AGL the vehicle slowed its decent to (guess of 3ft/s).
It is unlikely that this bird is surfacing a systemic issue that could result in a critical failure across the fleet.
SLA Breakout 128-117156-01 Rev B has the Over Voltage Protection pin of both E-Fuses set to ~35V.

would_settle_it.what: Software team analysis of the two VTOL watchdog resets (TLB refill exception address) and whether they line up with the climb abort / lift system fault message.
lrfFusion offset during descent to explain the early slow-down at about 100 ft.
Bench test of the scrapped center wing VTOL AP for hardware faults that could cause memory exceptions.

reasoning: The VTOL log shows two watchdog resets caused by a simple_tlb_refill_exception, one at the transition to fixed wing, the only such WDT known on 1.55.03, and Cody found the lrfFusion value offset. That narrows the symptoms to the VTOL AP software or the board it runs on plus an LRF fusion offset, but no cause for the exception was found and the wing was scrapped. The team closed it as Cannot Reproduce.
notes: Closed as Cannot Reproduce / Bermuda Triangle with an empty Root Cause field. Two symptoms on one flight (climb abort / WDT, and the odd descent). VXEP-723 (MCM resets from SLA breakout E-fuse) is a separate fault on the same aircraft, quoted only as context. FS2-2854 is a work list with no findings for this ticket.

event: PMA263 VXE688 at 29 Palms had numerous launch aborts before its later crash on landing (VXEP-611); this clone ticket tracks the launch aborts.
component: VTOL AP firmware 1.44 magnetometer ratio test (ImuConfig.magmargin 0.25)
failure_mode: old VTOL firmware's tight mag ratio margin (0.25) failed in local conditions, aborting launches; the margin was widened in VTOL 1.52 / GCS 6.0.12
contributing: operator downgraded XCOMM firmware mid-operations (4.68 to 4.60), an unsupported process
old spare center wing with serial number 1, possibly factory reset
possible uncalibrated mag or EMI in the training area

evidence.quote: Every VTOL CSV file from VXEP-611 would fail the ratio test at margin=0.25 and would pass with margin=0.6.
The attached image above clearly shows that all of the aborted launches were because they were running old VTOL software with limits that were failing in their environmental conditions.
Note: they downgraded the XCOMM firmware, which is an unsupported process in the middle of their launch aborts.
Three vehicles are missing firmware from last three releases. All vehicles are missing firmware from the last two releases.

team_root_cause: The aircraft was using outdated and mismatched software/firmware.
reasoning: Scott Hunter's analysis on VXEP-611 found every VTOL log would fail the mag ratio test at the 0.25 margin set in the 1.44 config files and pass at 0.6, the value delivered in later firmware. Dave Grosher confirms all the aborted launches came from those old VTOL limits. The team's root cause says outdated and mismatched software; the specific mechanism is the mag ratio margin in VTOL 1.44.
notes: Clone of VXEP-611, which covers the landing crash; the crash itself was not investigated in depth due to outdated firmware. The RMA-366 intake PDF has no extractable text (images only). The mismatch spreadsheet shows XCOMM 4.68 downgraded to 4.60 and VTOL 1.44 on 688. Did not read the two AD PDFs on FS2-2321 (release notes, not cause evidence); the RMA-366 form is blank.

event: Edge FLOPS VXE674 with an E140ZG2 gimbal auto-aborted its VTOL launch with an IMU failure message at about 50 ft, after starting to weathervane into the wind.
component: E140Z G2 gimbal (magnetic interference on the fixed wing AP magnetometer)
failure_mode: FWAP magnetometer heading disturbed by the gimbal, so FWAP and VTOL AP attitude disagreed and the launch auto-aborted as designed
contributing: gimbal ground loop through a conductive mount (VXEP-813)
weathervaning into the wind at about 50 ft
aircraft configuration (mount type) not confirmed

evidence.quote: Data shows attitude mismatch in xcomm logs, AP vs VTOL roll, pitch and yaw all show disagreement during launch, leading to abort.
Suspected mag interference due to E140 payload (awaiting confirmation on aircraft configuration).
At about 50 feet off the ground, the aircraft started to immediately weathervane into the wind.
When gimbal is moved in pan, it is obvious fw ap mag is impacted

team_root_cause: Fixed wing magnetometer interference due to E140ZG2 payload caused disagreement between FW and VTOL APs leading to launch abort.

would_settle_it.what: FWAP vs VTOL heading and mag field plot during launch to confirm the yaw disagreement came from the FW magnetometer.
Mag field magnitude and gimbal pan position at launch, and the mount type fitted on 674 that day.

reasoning: The XCOMM log shows FWAP and VTOL AP disagreeing on roll, pitch and yaw during launch, which triggered the designed abort. The engineer suspects the E140 gimbal disturbed the FW magnetometer, which matches the repeated interference shown on this same aircraft in VXEP-500, but the aircraft configuration was never confirmed. The abort worked as designed, so this is scored as narrowed to the degraded input (payload interference with the FW mag).
notes: Designed abort; scored on the degraded input. In VXEP-813, 674 with a 3D printed mount and G10 plate later passed mag checks and flew without mag issues on 18 Jan 2025, after this 13 Jan event, which supports the mount and ground loop link but does not prove it for this flight.
